base_prompt:
You author ORIGINAL Harbor tasks for evaluating a coding agent (GLM-5.3-flash with high reasoning, a text-only terminal agent). The agent sees instruction.md and the files in /app; hidden pytest tests in /tests then check /app/answer.txt. The agent CANNOT see images; it can only process files with code (Python 3.12 with Pillow is available to it).

FAMILY: grid-image-puzzle. Every task is an ORIGINAL single-player grid puzzle (never a public game: no sokoban, chess, checkers, go, minesweeper, 2048, tetris, lights-out, or similar). The boards exist ONLY as PNG images; the agent must decode them, apply the rules exactly, and list ALL minimal solutions.

WHY THIS DESIGN (measured on ~80 runs of this agent): it reliably solves tasks when it can check its own answers against something independent (it differential-tests against any runnable reference, reads binaries, and re-derives answers two ways). It fails tasks like this one in roughly 25-45% of attempts because nothing in the environment can confirm a decoded board or the final answer. Observed mistakes: reading a square board transposed (rows and columns swapped), misreading which edge a direction marker sits on, inferring a tile's meaning wrongly from the worked example, implementing the obvious version of a rule interaction (for example what happens when a forced movement is blocked), and listing only some of the minimal sequences. TARGET: the agent solves the task in 2-3 of 5 attempts. Do not add difficulty beyond what is described here: overly complex mechanics made the agent run out of time, which measures nothing.

PUZZLE DESIGN
- 4-6 precise movement rules, at least two of which interact. Good ingredients (combine 2-3 and invent your own twist): forced movement after a step (conveyors, ice, wind, currents) that repeats while on such tiles and has a stated stop rule; a limited resource (energy, fuel, keys) that some tiles refill or consume; tiles that change state when entered or left (crumbling floor, toggles, one-way doors); a move that is illegal for a stated reason other than walls (for example a loop in forced movement, or entering a tile with 0 resource); a goal that counts only under a stated condition.
- Moves are single letters (for example D, L, R, U) with a stated order used to sort move sequences as strings.
- Every rule needed to solve the boards is stated precisely in /app/docs/RULES.md. Nothing is left to guesswork except what the worked example shows (which tile looks like what).

IMAGES (decode-and-trust, strictly fair)
- fixtures/build_assets.py renders each board with Pillow: exactly CELL x CELL pixels per cell (CELL is a module constant between 16 and 24), no grid lines, no anti-aliasing (only ImageDraw.rectangle with solid fills), image size exactly (columns*CELL, rows*CELL), row 0 at the top. Every cell is drawn independently inside its own square: a base color for the tile type plus, for directional tiles, a solid marker bar along ONE edge (or a small solid square at a fixed position) that encodes the direction. The same tile character must always produce an identical pixel block, and different tile characters must produce different blocks.
- build_assets.py defines, as plain Python literals at module level: CELL; BOARDS = {"board1": [row strings], ...} with 4-5 boards, each 7-10 columns by 7-10 rows, at least half of them square; EXAMPLE = [row strings], a small NON-square board (for example 3x6 or 4x7) that contains EVERY tile character used on any board. It saves board images as "boardN.png" in its working directory (/app/fixtures) and the example as "../docs/example.png" (create that directory if needed). Use one-character tile codes ('.', '#', 'S', 'G', and so on).
- docs/RULES.md documents the rules, the CELL size, the drawing conventions above, and a PARTIAL legend: the colors of floor, wall, start, and goal only. It says that the remaining tile types appear in docs/example.png, that docs/example.txt shows the same board in text form, and states in words what each remaining character means (for example '>' is a conveyor pushing right, '+' is a charge pad) WITHOUT giving its color or marker. The pipeline writes docs/example.txt from EXAMPLE; do not write it yourself.
- The board text must not appear anywhere the agent can read: only in build_assets.py (deleted after the image build) and in the hidden tests.

BOARD QUALITY
- Each board is solvable; its minimum number of moves is 7-14; it has 2-20 minimal sequences (all must be listed); its minimal solutions exercise the interacting rules, so an agent that ignores or simplifies a rule gets a different answer; the start and goal are not adjacent. Think through the minimal solutions while designing each board.
- Open floor creates hundreds of equally short paths (a 7-move route through open floor can have 30+ orderings). Use walls and special tiles to channel movement into corridors so only a few routes are minimal; boards with more than 40 minimal sequences are rejected.

ANSWER FILE AND TESTS
- instruction.md: short and natural. Say: solve every board in /app/fixtures under the rules in /app/docs/RULES.md; write /app/answer.txt with one line per board, in board order: "boardN: <minimum number of moves> <all minimal move sequences, sorted ascending, separated by single spaces>"; the boards are only available as images; show one example line. (The pipeline appends a time-box paragraph.)
- Do NOT write answer.txt or BUG blocks: the pipeline creates the placeholder answer file and the per-board starter gaps, and fills the reference answers from the values your tests compute.
- tests/test_outputs.py: use the names BOARDS and EXAMPLE WITHOUT defining them (the pipeline injects the literals from build_assets.py at the top of the module). Implement the rules in an exact solver solve(rows) -> (min_moves, sorted list of all minimal move strings) using BFS over complete states (position plus every piece of changing state), collecting all shortest sequences, and treating illegal moves exactly as RULES.md says. Then define:
    def expected_line(name): returns f"{name}: {k} " + " ".join(seqs)
    def _answer_lines(): the non-blank, stripped lines of /app/answer.txt (assert the file exists)
    def test_line_count(): assert len(_answer_lines()) == len(BOARDS)
  and one test per board, exactly like:
    def test_board1():
        exp = expected_line("board1")
        record_expected("board1", exp)  # predefined helper: never define it; call it BEFORE asserting
        lines = [l for l in _answer_lines() if l.split(":")[0].strip() == "board1"]
        assert len(lines) == 1 and " ".join(lines[0].split()) == exp
  Tests must not decode images and must not import anything from /app.

The task must be original and different from the already-generated tasks listed by the user (different mechanic, different domain nouns).

OUTPUT FORMAT. Reply ONLY with these blocks, in this order. Write file contents verbatim; each block header is a line of its own.

=== META ===
{"slug": "short-kebab-case-descriptive-name", "summary": "one sentence describing the task"}
=== FILE instruction.md ===
<verbatim markdown>
=== FILE README.md ===
<short plain-language overview for humans; do not reveal answers or tile encodings>
=== FILE app/docs/RULES.md ===
<rules, drawing conventions, partial legend>
=== FILE fixtures/build_assets.py ===
<CELL, BOARDS, EXAMPLE literals and the renderer>
=== FILE tests/test_outputs.py ===
<verbatim pytest module>
=== END ===
measured_feedback:
MEASURED FEEDBACK FROM SOLVER RUNS:
Bug classes this agent MISSED often (prefer these kinds): inferred sub-cell encoding (missed 80% of 10 runs)
Bug classes this agent ALWAYS FIXED (avoid, or make far subtler): signed literal lexing (missed 0% of 5 runs); missing token type (missed 0% of 5 runs); floor vs truncating division (missed 0% of 5 runs); missing type check (missed 0% of 5 runs); prerelease precedence compared lexically (missed 0% of 5 runs); prerelease opt-in enabled by exclusion clause (missed 0% of 5 runs); revalidation skips eligibility rule (missed 0% of 5 runs); state not reset on backtrack (missed 0% of 5 runs)
Recent tasks were TOO EASY (mean 3.8/5 passes over the last 6). Use 5 bugs; every bug must need two interacting rules or a multi-step state sequence to surface.

SOLVER PROFILE (high-level strengths, weaknesses, and untested hypotheses learned from all runs; place difficulty in WEAKNESSES and HYPOTHESES, never rely on STRENGTHS; a 'bug' may also be a whole function body replaced by a docstring plus `raise NotImplementedError` when implementing from the spec is the intended difficulty):
# Solver profile p005

Built from 97 recorded probes at 2026-10-07 11:01.

## Strengths
- Reliably fixes multiple injected bugs in a single run across diverse task families, often resolving 4-8 bugs per task (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Employs extensive, ad-hoc verification strategies, writing comprehensive inline Python test scripts covering deterministic edge cases, randomized differential testing, and CLI integration checks (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Successfully handles complex stateful logic and boundary conditions, such as half-open interval overlaps, exact lease expiry boundaries, deduplication key lifecycle, rollback semantics, and correction ordering with secondary sort keys (evidence: 15+ tasks)
- Consistently compiles code and checks for syntax errors before submission, using `python3 -m py_compile` or similar commands (evidence: 20+ tasks)
- Successfully implements entire methods from specification rather than just localized bug fixes, including complex state machines with multiple transitions and interacting rules (evidence: 15+ tasks including Tasks 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28)

## Weaknesses
- Overconfident self-assessment: frequently claims implementation is complete and submits despite missing injected bugs, even after writing extensive tests that fail to cover the specific defect (evidence: 8+ tasks including Tasks 1, 4, 6, 11, 12, 13, 15, 25)
- Struggles with binary protocol field parsing where multi-byte integers require correct byte-order interpretation; writes tests with small values that don't reveal byte-order errors, then claims success (evidence: 3 tasks — Tasks 7, 25, 30)

## Hypotheses
- Struggles when verification tests don't exercise specific rule interactions in stateful protocols -> Design a task where two independent rules interact non-obviously (e.g., SYNC-frame suppression interacts with sequence-number acceptance, so a SYNC with seq==next_seq must not increment next_seq), and the agent's typical per-rule testing misses the cross-rule behavior.
- Struggles with state machines where error recovery has side effects that must occur before state transition -> Implement a decoder where an invalid byte sequence must trigger a side effect (e.g., increment an error counter, set a resynced flag) and then the same invalid byte is re-interpreted as the start of a new valid sequence, rather than being discarded.
- Struggles with protocol specifications where the same field has different semantics depending on frame type flags; tests exercising only one frame type miss behavior specific to others -> Design a protocol where a sequence number field is interpreted differently for SYNC vs DATA frames (e.g., SYNC frames use seq for resynchronization but don't deliver messages), and require tests that specifically exercise each frame type's handling of that field.
- Struggles with visual image decoding tasks combined with complex rule systems; imprecise pixel-to-symbol mapping cascades into rule-application errors that are hard to isolate and debug -> Design a task requiring both pixel-accurate image decoding (with ambiguous color boundaries or non-standard cell sizes) and multi-rule simulation, where a single misidentified cell propagates into incorrect rule outcomes across many test cases.

## Guidance
Place difficulty in binary field parsing (multi-byte integers with specific byte order) and cross-rule interactions in stateful protocols, as the agent's overconfidence leads it to submit without catching these. Design tasks where the failing test for a missed bug requires using values where byte order matters (e.g., sequence numbers >= 256) or exercising two rules together (e.g., SYNC suppression + sequence acceptance). Visual image decoding combined with complex rule systems also exploits a weakness, as decoding errors cascade into rule failures. Do not rely on simple boundary off-by-one errors, missing imports, single-rule violations, or whole-method implementation difficulty alone, as the agent handles these reliably. Consider combining binary parsing errors with rule-interaction bugs in the same task to maximize the chance the agent's tests miss at least one defect.
